title: Are open-plan offices a mistake?

turns.speaker: Will
turns.text: They're knocking the partitions out on our floor. Open plan, hot desks, collaboration, the whole vocabulary.

turns.speaker: Jonah
turns.text: There's that study where two firms went open plan and face-to-face conversation dropped by about seventy per cent.

turns.speaker: Jonah
turns.text: Dropped. Email and messaging went up instead. People put headphones on and built a wall out of software.

turns.speaker: Will
turns.text: That matches everything I've watched happen. You don't start a conversation when nine people can hear it.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: I'd say it depends enormously on the work, though. A design team genuinely does better overhearing each other. Anyone writing anything doesn't.

turns.speaker: Jonah
turns.text: So the failure is treating one layout as correct for every kind of task.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: And the real reason is usually the floor plan costs less per head. Collaboration is the word you put on the slide afterwards.

turns.speaker: Will
turns.text: Which is fine. I'd just rather someone said it.

turns.speaker: Jonah
turns.text: The hot desking part is separate and I think it's worse. You lose the small things, knowing who sits where, noticing somebody's had a bad week.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: That's the invisible cost. It doesn't show up anywhere until people start leaving.

turns.speaker: Will
turns.text: The compromise everyone lands on is zones. Quiet floor, loud floor, rooms you can actually book.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: Which costs more than the open plan it replaced, so it tends to arrive after the damage.

points: A workplace is moving to open plan with hot desking.
Jonah cites research where face-to-face conversation fell by about seventy per cent after the change, replaced by email and messaging.
Will agrees people avoid conversations others can overhear.
Ana argues suitability depends on the work, helping design teams and harming anyone writing.
She adds that the real driver is cost per head, with collaboration used as justification afterwards.
Jonah separates hot desking as a further harm, losing incidental social knowledge; they agree zoned offices work but cost more and usually arrive too late.
